blocks.text: A chest drainage system, commonly called an underwater seal drain (UWSD), is a closed drainage apparatus connected to a chest tube to remove air, blood, pus or other fluid from the pleural cavity.
Its purpose is to help restore the normal negative pressure relationship between the pleural cavity and the lung, allowing the lung to re-expand when the underlying condition permits.

items.text: Classification: Thoracic drainage and respiratory support equipment.
Principle: A one-way water seal permits air to escape from the pleural space while preventing atmospheric air from flowing back into the chest.
Common indications: Pneumothorax, haemothorax, pleural effusion and empyema, depending on the clinical situation.
Key identifying features: Drainage tubing, a collection chamber and a water-seal chamber; some systems also include a suction-control chamber.
Pneumothorax: Evacuation of air from the pleural space.
Haemothorax: Drainage of blood following trauma or another cause.
Pleural effusion: Drainage of pleural fluid when chest-tube drainage is indicated.
Empyema: Drainage of infected pleural fluid as part of appropriate treatment.
Postoperative thoracic care: Drainage of air and fluid following selected thoracic or cardiac procedures.
Monitoring: Assessment of drainage volume, character and trends, as well as relevant air-leak indicators.

blocks.text: OSCE distinction: The chest tube enters the pleural space; the underwater seal drainage system remains outside the patient and connects to the tube.
A. Collection chamber
Collects drained blood, fluid or other pleural contents. Graduated markings allow measurement of drainage volume.
B. Water-seal chamber
Acts as a one-way valve. It allows air to leave the pleural space while preventing atmospheric air from returning through the drainage system.
C. Suction-control chamber
Present in some systems. In a traditional wet-suction system, the prescribed water level helps regulate suction. Dry-suction systems use a mechanical regulator instead.
D. Connecting tubing
Carries air and fluid from the chest tube to the drainage unit. It should remain securely connected and free from kinks or obstruction.
E. Stand or hanger
Keeps the drainage unit upright and below the level of the patient’s chest, reducing the risk of backflow.

items.text: Provides continuous drainage of air and fluid.
The water seal reduces the risk of air re-entering the pleural space through the drain.
Allows monitoring of fluid volume and appearance.
Water-seal movement and bubbling may provide useful information about respiratory mechanics and air leaks.
Can facilitate lung re-expansion when drainage is effective and the underlying condition allows.
Portable systems can allow patient mobility when clinically appropriate.
Incorrect setup can compromise drainage or allow air to enter the pleural space.
Tubing may kink, become blocked or become disconnected.
Infection, bleeding, pain and organ injury can occur from chest-tube insertion or maintenance.
Excessive or inappropriate suction may be harmful.
Drainage volume alone does not establish whether the lung has re-expanded.
Bubbling and fluid movement must be interpreted in context; neither finding alone confirms that the drain is functioning correctly.
The system requires regular observation and appropriate documentation.

blocks.title: Before handling or checking the system:

items.text: Perform hand hygiene and use appropriate personal protective equipment.
Explain the procedure to the patient where possible.
Confirm the prescribed drainage arrangement and whether suction is required.
Check the integrity of the unit, connections and tubing.
Ensure the unit is upright and below chest level.
Confirm the water-seal and suction settings against the manufacturer’s instructions and prescription.
Assess the patient’s respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, work of breathing, chest movement and haemodynamic status.
Check the insertion site and dressing for bleeding, leakage, infection or displacement.

blocks.text: Critical safety precautions

items.text: Do not routinely clamp a chest drain. Clamping can trap air and precipitate or worsen a tension pneumothorax, particularly when an air leak is present.
Do not routinely strip or aggressively milk the tubing; these actions may generate excessive negative pressure and should only be performed under a specific protocol.
Do not lift the collection unit above chest level.
Do not disconnect the system casually or manipulate the tube without appropriate clinical justification.
If the patient deteriorates, assess the patient immediately and escalate urgently rather than focusing only on the apparatus.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. How to use it — step-by-step OSCE demonstration

blocks.text: This is a guide to demonstrating the equipment and checking an established drain. Insertion of a chest tube is a separate invasive procedure performed by appropriately trained clinicians.
Step 1: Introduce and assess
Introduce yourself, confirm the patient’s identity, explain your assessment and obtain consent if possible. Assess the patient’s respiratory and haemodynamic status.
Step 2: Inspect the drainage unit
Identify the collection chamber, water seal and suction-control mechanism if present. Confirm that the unit is upright and configured according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Step 3: Check the tubing
Trace the tubing from the patient to the unit. Look for disconnections, kinks, dependent loops, compression or visible obstruction. Do not manipulate the tube unnecessarily.
Step 4: Observe the water seal
Look for respiratory fluctuation, sometimes called tidaling. Bubbling may occur when air is escaping through the system. Interpret these findings according to the clinical context and drain type.
Step 5: Measure the drainage

Record the volume, colour and character of the drainage and compare it with previous observations. Escalate sudden large-volume drainage or fresh blood according to the clinical situation and local protocol.
Step 6: Inspect the patient and insertion site
Assess the dressing, surrounding skin, respiratory effort, chest movement and oxygen saturation. Look for signs of infection, subcutaneous emphysema or worsening pneumothorax.
Step 7: Document and escalate
Record the observations, drainage output, water-seal findings, suction settings where applicable and the patient’s clinical condition. Escalate any abnormal findings promptly.

rows: Fluid level fluctuates with respiration
Respiratory transmission of pressure changes; may be expected in a patent system.
Intermittent bubbling
May occur as air escapes, particularly with pneumothorax.
Continuous bubbling in the water seal
May indicate an ongoing air leak from the patient or a leak in the system; assess promptly.
No fluctuation
May occur after lung re-expansion or with certain drainage systems, but may also reflect obstruction, kinking or disconnection.
Sudden cessation of previously observed bubbling
May indicate that the leak has resolved, but obstruction or another system problem must also be considered.

blocks.text: Examiner’s point: Never interpret a single observation in isolation. Assess the patient first and check the entire drainage system.
The drainage system itself has no simple universal contraindication; the decision to insert a chest tube depends on the underlying condition and clinical circumstances.

rows: Tube blockage or kinking
Reduced drainage, altered water-seal behaviour or clinical deterioration
Disconnection or system leak
Loss of system integrity, possible air entry
Tube displacement
Change in external tube position, leakage or reduced effectiveness
Infection
Fever, erythema, discharge or increasing local pain
Bleeding
Fresh blood, rapidly increasing output or haemodynamic instability
Subcutaneous emphysema
Crackling sensation under the skin
Tension pneumothorax
Sudden respiratory or cardiovascular deterioration; an emergency
Re-expansion pulmonary oedema
New respiratory distress and hypoxaemia after re-expansion in susceptible patients

blocks.text: Large or rapidly increasing bloody drainage, sudden respiratory deterioration, suspected tension pneumothorax or major system disruption requires immediate clinical assessment and escalation.
Potentially reassuring findings

items.text: Secure connections and patent, unkinked tubing.
Drainage consistent with the patient’s condition and clinical trajectory.
Appropriate water-seal and suction settings.
Respiratory findings and oxygenation that are stable or improving.
No new signs of infection, bleeding or subcutaneous emphysema.

blocks.text: Concerning findings

items.text: Sudden increase in fresh blood drainage.
New or worsening breathlessness, hypoxaemia or haemodynamic instability.
Continuous water-seal bubbling suggesting an air leak.
Sudden cessation of drainage when obstruction is suspected.
Disconnection, displacement or a damaged drainage unit.
New subcutaneous emphysema or signs of infection.

blocks.text: “The patient has a chest drain connected to an underwater seal drainage system. The unit is upright and below chest level, and the tubing is connected without visible kinking. I would assess the water-seal behaviour, prescribed suction settings and drainage volume and character, then correlate these findings with the patient’s respiratory status. I would escalate any suspected air leak, obstruction, bleeding or clinical deterioration.”

items.text: Use appropriately sized chest tubes and drainage equipment for the child’s clinical indication and body size.
Secure the tube carefully because children may inadvertently pull or displace it.
Provide age-appropriate pain relief and explain the equipment to the child and caregiver.
Monitor respiratory status closely; children may deteriorate rapidly.
Record drainage carefully and interpret output according to the child’s size, condition and clinical trajectory.
Ensure any suction setting is specifically prescribed and appropriate for the patient and device.
If a drain becomes disconnected or displaced, follow the emergency protocol and obtain urgent senior assistance. Do not improvise a repair or clamp the tube without appropriate direction.

Measure and describe the output.
Respiratory status
Assess breathing, oxygenation and clinical stability.
Air leak
Observe bubbling and investigate unexpected changes.
Integrity
Check the tubing, connections and insertion site.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Common OSCE questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the principle of an underwater seal drain?
It provides a one-way pathway for air and fluid to leave the pleural space while preventing atmospheric air from returning through the water seal.
Q2. Why must the drainage unit be below chest level?
This reduces the risk of fluid flowing backwards towards the patient and supports gravity drainage.
Q3. What is tidaling?
It is respiratory fluctuation of the water level in the water-seal chamber, reflecting pressure changes transmitted through the system. Its presence or absence must be interpreted in context.
Q4. What does continuous bubbling mean?
It may indicate a persistent air leak from the patient or a leak in the drainage system. I would assess the patient, inspect the connections and escalate according to the clinical protocol.
Q5. Why should a chest drain not be routinely clamped?
Clamping can prevent air from escaping and cause a tension pneumothorax when an ongoing air leak is present.
Q6. What would you do if drainage suddenly stopped?

I would assess the patient immediately, inspect the tubing for kinks or obstruction, review the water-seal behaviour and seek urgent assistance if obstruction or clinical deterioration is suspected. I would not strip the tubing or manipulate the system indiscriminately.
Q7. What is the difference between a water-seal chamber and a suction-control chamber?
The water seal acts as a one-way valve. The suction-control chamber or mechanism regulates the prescribed negative pressure when suction is being used.
Q8. What would you do if the patient suddenly became breathless?

I would assess airway, breathing and circulation, provide urgent support according to the emergency protocol, check the drain and escalate immediately. I would consider tension pneumothorax among the possible causes.
Common mistakes

items.text: Placing the drainage unit above chest level.
Failing to inspect the tubing from patient to unit.
Confusing the water-seal chamber with the collection chamber.
Assuming all bubbling is abnormal.
Assuming absence of tidaling always means obstruction.
Routinely clamping, stripping or milking the tube.
Ignoring sudden fresh blood drainage.
Assessing the apparatus without assessing the patient.

blocks.text: Examiner tips

items.text: Start by assessing the patient, not just the equipment.
Identify the collection chamber, water seal and suction-control mechanism.
Explain the significance and limitations of bubbling and tidaling.
State that the unit should remain upright and below chest level.
Explicitly mention that routine clamping is unsafe.
Document drainage volume and character, respiratory observations and any escalation.

blocks.text: Practice station
Scenario
A patient with a pneumothorax has a chest tube connected to an underwater seal drainage system. During your ward assessment, you notice continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber.
Your tasks

items.text: Identify the equipment and explain its principle.
Name its main components.
Explain two possible causes of continuous bubbling.
Describe your immediate assessment and next steps.
State two important safety precautions.
